title: Student discounts: the money is in the asking
description: A student card is a quiet discount machine — but only where you actually present it. The habit is simply to ask, everywhere, every time.

body.heading: Where discounts hide
paragraphs: Software, transport, museums, cinemas, hairdressers, bookshops, and many cafés offer student rates that are not always advertised at the till. Verification schemes and student cards exist for online shopping too, often covering technology and clothing.

The discounts are usually modest — 10% here, a cheaper ticket there — but they apply to spending you were doing anyway. Ten percent back across a year of ordinary purchases is a week or more of free living.

body.heading: Ask like it is normal
paragraphs: The entire technique is one sentence: "Do you offer a student discount?" Asked politely, the worst answer is a friendly no. Shops expect the question; students who never ask are simply donating the difference.
Keep your student ID with your payment card so the question costs no effort. And check expiry dates on discount accounts — renewing the verification each year keeps the savings switched on.

body.heading: Discounts are not a reason to buy
paragraphs: A student price is still a price. The discount improves a purchase you had already decided was worth it; it does not promote a maybe into a yes. Judge the reduced price exactly as you would any other, with the same cost-per-use maths.

Watch for the opposite trap as well: spending more to reach a discount threshold, or choosing the dearer shop because it offers 10% off. Ten percent off an expensive price can still lose to the ordinary price elsewhere — compare the final figures, not the percentages.

takeaway: Carry your student ID beside your card and ask for the discount everywhere. Modest percentages on ordinary spending quietly add up to real money across a year.
